intro:
These exercises move you from slogans to contracts. The chapter's central claim is that once work crosses a process boundary, the compiler stops protecting you, and the guarantees you actually have are the ones you build: at-least-once delivery, leases with visibility timeouts, classified retries, idempotent completion, and traceable recovery. Each exercise pins one of those guarantees down to a concrete shape in Rust worker and queue code, the same way Examples 1 and 2 in the chapter do.

The through-line is the separation between two layers that beginners conflate. The transport layer decides how many times your handler runs; the application layer decides what a duplicate run means for your durable side effects. Exercises 1 through 3 establish that separation and implement the minimal mechanics. Exercises 4 and 5 centralize the policies (retry, dead-lettering, tracing) that tend to get copy-pasted into every handler. Exercise 6 asks you to assemble the whole control plane for a realistic media pipeline, where a long-running GPU step makes leasing discipline non-negotiable.

exerciseSolutions.title: Classify delivery semantics and idempotency obligations
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The point of this exercise is to keep two questions apart that sound like one. Delivery semantics is a transport property: how many times the queue may hand the same logical task to a handler. Business side-effect semantics is an application property: what happens to durable state when the handler runs twice. A queue can promise at-least-once delivery, but only your code can decide whether a second run is harmless. Claiming "exactly-once" as a queue property by itself is the slogan the chapter warns against; honest exactly-once is something you construct from at-least-once delivery plus idempotent side effects.

Thumbnail regeneration is the workload that can tolerate occasional loss and may accept at-most-once behavior. A dropped regeneration just means a stale or missing thumbnail until the next trigger; nothing is corrupted, and the cost of a lost run is cosmetic. It is also naturally repeat-safe in the other direction, because regenerating writes one deterministic final image and overwrites whatever was there. If you had to pick the workload whose final state is a single deterministic overwrite, this is it.

Billing capture is the workload that must tolerate replay and therefore needs explicit idempotency even under at-least-once delivery. Capturing a payment twice double-charges a customer, so a second delivery of the same task must be suppressed. This is the workload that forces you to define a durable dedupe boundary: an idempotency key (for example the order or invoice ID) recorded in the same durable transaction that performs the charge, so the second attempt sees the key already present and becomes a no-op. The dedupe state has to be durable and co-located with the side effect, not held in a worker's memory.

A cache warmup is loss-tolerant like the thumbnail job (a missed warmup just means a cold cache and a slow first request) and is repeat-safe by overwrite, so it sits comfortably at at-most-once or unguarded at-least-once. A periodic analytics refresh is the more interesting middle case: if it recomputes one deterministic snapshot and overwrites it, replay is harmless; but if it appends or accumulates, a replay double-counts, and then it joins billing in needing an explicit checkpoint or run-ID boundary. The lesson is that you classify from business tolerance and the structure of the side effect, not from the transport label printed on the queue.
criteria: Delivery semantics (how many times the handler runs) is kept distinct from business side-effect semantics (what a rerun does to durable state).
Thumbnail/cache warmup are identified as naturally repeat-safe overwrites; billing capture is identified as needing explicit durable dedupe state.
Exactly-once is treated as constructed from at-least-once delivery plus idempotency, never asserted as a standalone queue guarantee.

exerciseSolutions.title: Read a lease timeline like an incident reviewer
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Read this timeline the way the chapter reads its lease lifecycle diagram: the duplicate execution is not a bug, it is the recovery mechanism working as designed. The event that makes duplicate execution normal is Worker A's lease expiry. When A claimed task-7 the queue hid it for the visibility-timeout window. A then went quiet past its deadline, so the queue concluded A was gone and made task-7 visible again, which let Worker B reclaim it legitimately. From the queue's point of view there is now exactly one valid owner (B), but A never learned it lost the lease, so A finishing later is an expected consequence of at-least-once delivery, not a surprise. Lease expiry is a recovery event, not a correctness defect by itself.

The correctness defect appears only if the completion path is not idempotent. Two successes are reported (A's late one and B's), and if completion simply applies the side effect each time, the work runs twice. So the fix is structural: completion state must live at the durable side-effect boundary, recorded atomically with the effect itself, keyed by the task's stable identity. In the chapter's example that is the `completed` set keyed by task ID, and `finish_once` returns whether this caller was the first to record it. The first reporter (whichever of A or B records first) wins and applies the effect; the second reporter sees the key already present and its completion becomes a harmless no-op. The dedupe record cannot live in a worker's local memory, because the two workers do not share memory; it has to live in the durable store next to the effect.

To reduce replay without slowing recovery, the lever is the visibility timeout relative to real handler time, plus heartbeats. A timeout that is too short relative to how long the handler actually takes will expire leases on healthy, still-working workers and cause needless reclaims; lengthening it globally just delays recovery when a worker truly dies. The better answer is heartbeat-based lease renewal: a worker that is still making progress periodically extends its lease, so a slow-but-alive worker keeps ownership while a dead worker's lease still expires quickly. That decouples "how long real work takes" from "how fast we recover from a crash."

The metric that tells you the lease duration is badly matched to handler time is the lease-expiry / redelivery rate, ideally read against the distribution of actual handler durations. A redelivery rate that climbs while almost no workers are actually crashing is the signature of a visibility timeout set below the p95 or p99 handler time: leases are expiring on workers that are simply slow, not dead. Task age (time from enqueue to terminal completion) is the companion signal, because excessive reclaims inflate it. Watch those two together and you can tune the timeout, or switch to heartbeats, with evidence instead of guesswork.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Idempotent completion keyed by task ID: whichever worker records first wins, the other's success is a no-op.
criteria: The duplicate-execution path is explained concretely as the consequence of A's lease expiry and B's legitimate reclaim, with A unaware it lost the lease.
Completion/dedupe state is placed at the durable side-effect boundary, keyed by stable task identity, so only one success is applied.
Tuning and observability are addressed via visibility-timeout vs handler-time, heartbeat renewal, and the lease-expiry/redelivery rate plus task-age signals.

exerciseSolutions.title: Build a lease-based worker with idempotent completion
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The starter code has exactly two defects, and both are inversions of the intended condition. In `requeue_if_timed_out`, the guard reads `if self.now < deadline`, which requeues a task while its lease is still valid and drops it once the lease has expired, the precise opposite of what a visibility timeout means. A task should return to visibility only when the current time has reached or passed the deadline, so the condition must be `if self.now >= deadline`. With `now = 6` and `deadline = 5` the corrected guard fires and the task is redelivered.

In `finish_once`, the stub always returns `false` and never records anything, so completion is neither performed nor idempotent. The clean repair leans on the standard library: `HashSet::insert` returns `true` when the key was newly inserted and `false` when it was already present. Returning that value directly makes the method self-describing: the first completion of a given task ID returns `true` (this caller applied the effect), and every subsequent attempt returns `false` (a harmless duplicate). No extra flag, no second lookup, no branch. This is the "calmest duplicate signal" the hint points at.

Keeping all of this on one `Queue` struct, rather than scattering `visible`, `completed`, and `now` into globals, is what lets ownership do the bookkeeping. The methods take `&mut self`, so the borrow checker guarantees no two code paths mutate the queue's state concurrently through this owner, and the lifetime `&'static str` keys mean the completion set borrows nothing it could outlive. The struct is the durable boundary in miniature: redelivery state and completion state live together, the way they must when the real version is backed by a database row rather than a `HashSet`.

With both fixes the driver in `main` produces the lab's expected output: the task is claimed, time advances past the deadline, `requeue_if_timed_out` returns it to visibility, the redelivery is claimed again, the first `finish_once` records it, and the second returns `false` so `!duplicate_apply` prints `true`. `completed.len()` is `1` because the idempotent insert collapses the two completion attempts into one recorded effect.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Two one-line repairs: invert the timeout guard, and return the HashSet insert result as the duplicate signal.
criteria: Timed-out work requeues correctly: the guard is `now >= deadline`, so the expired task returns to visibility.
Completion is idempotent: `finish_once` returns the `HashSet::insert` result, recording once and reporting later attempts as duplicates.
The lab prints `redelivered = task-1`, `completed = 1`, `duplicate = true`, matching the expected output.

exerciseSolutions.title: Centralize distributed retries and poison-task policy
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is duplicated, divergent retry logic plus a missing terminal exit. Three handlers each carry their own retry loop with slightly different attempt limits, which means the system has three subtly different reliability behaviors and no single place to reason about or change them. Worse, every permanent validation error is requeued, so a malformed payload that can never succeed cycles forever, consuming a worker slot on each pass and inflating the redelivery rate. The chapter's state machine names the missing piece directly: there must be a one-way exit to DeadLetter, or the system will requeue a permanently broken task indefinitely.

The repair is to give retry one home: a shared `RetryPolicy` that owns four facts. First, max attempts, the visible attempt budget that bounds how many times any task may be re-tried. Second, the set of retryable failure classes, the classification that decides which failures even qualify for another attempt. Third, backoff, so retries are spaced (exponential with jitter) rather than hammering a struggling dependency. Fourth, terminal routing, the decision of where a failure goes when it is non-retryable or has exhausted its budget, namely the dead-letter queue. Centralizing these means all three handlers share one reliability behavior, and changing the policy is a one-line edit rather than three out-of-sync ones.

The failures that should be dead-lettered immediately are the permanent ones: validation errors, schema violations, deserialization failures, unknown-tenant or authorization rejections, anything where the same input will deterministically fail again. Retrying these wastes capacity and hides the real problem. Transient failures, such as a timeout against a throttled dependency, a connection reset, or a 503, are the only ones that earn a retry, and only until the attempt budget is spent; after that they too are dead-lettered so they stop circulating. This is exactly the chapter's discipline: classify before you retry, and separate transient retryable failure from permanent terminal failure.

The boundary between local in-process retry and queue-level requeue is the one teams blur most. Fast, in-handler retries (a couple of immediate attempts against a flaky local call, within one lease) are fine for sub-second transients and never touch the queue. But anything that needs real backoff, survives a worker crash, or counts against a durable attempt budget belongs at the queue level, because only the queue's redelivery and DLQ routing are durable across worker death. In-process bookkeeping ends where durability begins. Finally, the whole thing is testable without a broker: make the policy a pure function from a classified error and an attempt count to a `RetryDecision` (`Retry { after }`, `DeadLetter`, or `Drop`), and exercise it with a table-driven test plus assertions that terminal errors route to the DLQ. The transport stays mocked; the policy is just data in, decision out.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: One shared RetryPolicy as a pure decision function: permanent errors dead-letter immediately, transient ones retry within a budget.
criteria: Retry classification and the visible attempt budget are centralized in one RetryPolicy that owns max attempts, retryable classes, backoff, and terminal routing.
Transient retryable failures are separated from permanent terminal failures, with permanent ones dead-lettered immediately so poison tasks stop circulating.
A test strategy is named: a table-driven classification test plus DLQ-routing assertions against the pure decision function, with no live broker.

exerciseSolutions.title: Trace a distributed task graph end to end
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is that the trace shows handler spans but is blind to everything between them, and across a queue "between them" is where most of the latency lives. The chapter's framing is the key: in one process a stack trace carries the causal chain for free, but across a queue there is no shared stack, so the causal chain has to be carried inside the message itself. A trace that only instruments the handler body silently assumes the in-process model and loses the queue wait, the fan-out lineage, and the fan-in join entirely. Each handler looks fast while the pipeline as a whole is slow, and nobody can attribute the slowness.

The fix begins with the task envelope. Every message must carry a stable set of IDs independent of its business payload: a `trace_id` shared by the whole graph, a `span_id` for this node, and a `parent_span_id` (or, for fan-in nodes, a set of parent IDs) recording lineage. It should also carry a stable `task_id`/`message_id` for idempotency and an `enqueued_at` timestamp. The `trace_id` ties the whole DAG together so you can query one pipeline run; the parent linkage is what reconstructs fetch -> parse -> { enrich, store } -> notify as a causal tree rather than a pile of unrelated spans.

Parent-child lineage has to be recorded at the structural nodes specifically. At a fan-out node (parse spawning both enrich and store), each child envelope inherits the parent's span as its `parent_span_id`, so the two branches are visibly siblings under parse. At a fan-in node (notify, which depends on enrich and store), the node records multiple parents, so the trace shows it as a true join and you can see which input arrived last. Without recording lineage at exactly these branch and join points, fan-out looks like duplication and fan-in looks like a node with a mysteriously late start.

Queue wait must be promoted to a first-class trace concept, not left implicit. Stamp `enqueued_at` when the task is published and `claimed_at` when a worker picks it up; the interval between them is a dedicated "queue wait" span (or at least a measured event) that sits before the handler span. That single addition is what turns a cheap-to-run, expensive-to-wait task from invisible into obvious, and it is the chapter's point that you separate queue wait from handler time before you optimize anything. Finally, the graph-specific signal that tells you the bottleneck is aggregation rather than worker execution is reducer lag, the time the fan-in node spends waiting for its slowest input after its other inputs are already done. High reducer lag with low per-handler time means the critical path runs through the join, not through any one worker; frontier size (how many nodes are ready but unscheduled) and end-to-end critical-path time round out the graph-level view that a flat per-handler profile cannot give you.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Envelope carries trace_id and parent lineage; queue wait is measured as its own span, distinct from handler time.
criteria: The envelope carries a stable task/message ID plus trace lineage fields (trace_id, span_id, parent_span_ids), recorded at fan-out and fan-in nodes.
Queue wait is represented as a first-class trace/metric concept (enqueued_at to claimed_at), separate from handler time.
A graph-specific profiling signal is named: reducer lag at the join, with frontier size and critical-path time as companions, to locate aggregation bottlenecks.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose queue topology, aggregation, tracing, and profiling for a production task service
exerciseSolutions.solution:
This is the full control plane for `upload -> transcode variants -> scan -> persist metadata -> notify`, and the design is driven by three asymmetries in the workload: uploads are bursty, transcode is a long-running GPU step, and operators demand replay and forensics. Each of those pushes a specific structural decision.

Queue topology: split by stage, and shard the expensive stage by resource. Give transcode its own queue (and its own worker pool bound to GPU hosts) separate from the CPU-bound scan, metadata, and notify stages. The reason is failure and resource isolation, the decoupling the chapter calls the whole point of a task queue: a GPU outage or a backlog of large transcodes must not block fast metadata writes or notifications, and bursty uploads should land in a buffer queue that absorbs the spike rather than overwhelming the GPU pool directly. Within transcode, fan out one queue message per variant (1080p, 720p, thumbnail) so variants run in parallel and a single failed variant retries independently instead of failing the whole transcode. That is the deliberate shard split: transcode-variants gets its own boundary because it is both the most expensive stage and the one with independent sub-units.

Leases for the long step: renew, do not lengthen. The GPU transcode is exactly the case the chapter calls out: a long-running specialist is a stronger argument for leasing discipline than for a longer global timeout. Lengthening the visibility timeout globally to cover the worst-case transcode would delay recovery for every other stage when a worker dies. Instead, transcode workers send heartbeats that renew the lease while the job is genuinely progressing (for example, advancing through encode frames), and the queue keeps a short base timeout so a crashed worker is still reclaimed quickly. A worker that stops heartbeating, crashed or hung, loses its lease and the variant is redelivered; a worker that is slow but alive keeps ownership. Pair this with idempotent persistence keyed by `(upload_id, variant)` so a reclaim-then-late-finish race writes each variant exactly once.

Aggregation and failure isolation: completion is a counting join, not a guess. The notify stage fires only when persist-metadata has recorded all required variants plus a clean scan result for one `upload_id`. Concretely, maintain a durable per-upload completion record (a set of finished variant keys); each variant's persist step idempotently inserts its key, and the coordinator checks "have all required variants plus scan landed?" after each insert. This is the chapter's ready-frontier idea applied to a join: the graph is complete when the fan-in node's dependency set is fully satisfied, recorded durably so the decision survives a coordinator restart. The failure-isolation rule: classify transcode failures, and route GPU-specific transient failures (OOM on a host, driver hiccup) to a dedicated retry lane with its own bounded concurrency and backoff, so a burst of slow GPU retries cannot consume the workers that healthy uploads need; permanent failures (corrupt input, unsupported codec) go straight to a DLQ for forensic inspection rather than recirculating.

Observability required before rollout: at least queue age per stage (time from enqueue to claim, which surfaces a starving GPU lane early), redelivery / lease-expiry rate per stage (a climbing transcode redelivery rate means the heartbeat or timeout is mistuned), reducer lag at the notify join (how long notify waits for its slowest input, distinguishing an aggregation bottleneck from slow workers), trace lineage carried in every envelope (trace_id plus parent spans so an incident reviewer can replay one upload's full DAG), and duplicate-suppression hits (how often idempotent completion absorbed a replay, which both proves the dedupe works and quantifies how much redelivery is actually happening). These are not nice-to-haves; the chapter's hardest-bug warning is that the failure is usually a silently wrong recovery model, and these are the signals that make the recovery model visible before the first incident rather than during it.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Per-stage control plane: transcode gets its own sharded queue with renew-on-progress leases; five observability hooks are required pre-rollout.
criteria: At least one deliberate queue/shard split is chosen: transcode gets its own queue and pool, fanned out per variant, isolated from CPU-bound stages.
A lease/renewal policy is defined for the long GPU step: short base timeout with heartbeat-based renew-on-progress rather than a longer global timeout.
One aggregation rule (durable per-upload completion set gating notify) and one failure-isolation rule (dedicated GPU retry lane plus DLQ for permanent failures) are described.
At least three observability hooks are named: queue age, redelivery rate, reducer lag, trace lineage, and duplicate-suppression hits.

labSolution.explanation:
The lab models a lease timeout followed by an idempotent completion, the same lifecycle as Example 1 reduced to its two essential mechanics. The driver pushes `task-1`, claims it (the first worker), then sets `now = 6` to simulate the worker going quiet past a deadline of `5`. The completed program fixes the two stubs in the starter: `requeue_if_timed_out` now guards on `self.now >= deadline`, so because `6 >= 5` the task returns to visibility, and `finish_once` now returns `self.completed.insert(task.id)` instead of a hardcoded `false`.

With the timeout guard corrected, the second `claim` succeeds and `redelivery.id` is `task-1`, printing `redelivered = task-1`. The first `finish_once` inserts `task-1` into the `completed` set and returns `true` (recorded as `_first_apply`); the second `finish_once` on the same redelivery finds the key already present and returns `false`, so `duplicate_apply` is `false` and `!duplicate_apply` prints `duplicate = true`. Because the set insert is idempotent, the two completion attempts collapse to a single recorded effect, so `completed.len()` is `1` and the line prints `completed = 1`.

The design lesson is that the queue's recovery guarantee (lease expiry returns the task to visibility) and the application's correctness guarantee (idempotent completion) are separate and both required. Lease expiry alone would let the redelivered work run, but only the duplicate-safe `finish_once` keeps a second success from applying the effect twice. Both guarantees live on one `Queue` owner, so `&mut self` and the `'static` keys let ownership enforce that the redelivery and completion state stay consistent.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is at-least-once delivery the calm default assumption for distributed task systems?
reviewAnswers.answer: Because durable queues cannot safely do otherwise: after a worker claims a task and then stops responding, the queue has no way to know whether the work finished, so the safe move is to redeliver. That choice guarantees the task is not silently lost, at the cost of occasionally delivering it more than once. At-most-once would risk dropping work whenever a worker dies mid-task, and true exactly-once delivery is not something transport can provide on its own; so at-least-once is the honest, durable default, and your code supplies idempotency to make replays harmless.

reviewAnswers.question: What is the practical difference between a lease expiry and a processing bug?
reviewAnswers.answer: A lease expiry is a normal recovery event: the queue concluded a worker was unresponsive, so it reclaimed the task and made it visible again, which is exactly the mechanism that protects you from lost work when a machine dies. A processing bug is a defect in your handler or completion path. The two only intersect when the completion path is not idempotent: then the expected redelivery from a lease expiry causes a duplicate side effect, and what looks like a bug is really a missing idempotency guarantee, not a fault in the lease mechanism itself.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should retries and terminal failure paths be centralized instead of copied into each handler?
reviewAnswers.answer: Copying retry loops into each handler produces several divergent reliability behaviors, with subtly different attempt limits, backoff, and failure classification that no one can reason about or change in one place. Centralizing them into one policy gives the system a single, testable home for max attempts, which failures are retryable, backoff, and terminal (dead-letter) routing. It also ensures permanent failures, such as validation errors, are dead-lettered immediately rather than requeued forever by an ad-hoc handler branch, and it lets you test the policy as a pure decision function without a live broker.

reviewAnswers.question: What makes queue wait time a first-class profiling signal?
reviewAnswers.answer: Because a task can be cheap to run and expensive to wait for, and the in-process habit of profiling the handler body misses that entirely. In a distributed system, time spent sitting in the queue before a worker even starts is often the dominant latency, and it is invisible unless you measure it explicitly, for example by stamping enqueue and claim times and treating the interval as its own span. Separating queue wait from handler time is the first number to look at, because optimizing the hot function does nothing if the real cost is a starved or backlogged queue.

reviewAnswers.question: Why does a large task graph need explicit lineage and aggregation policy rather than one flat success counter?
reviewAnswers.answer: A graph is a fan-out followed by a fan-in, and a single counter cannot express which nodes a join depends on or whether the right set has completed. You need explicit lineage (trace_id plus parent spans carried in each envelope) because there is no shared stack across queues to reconstruct the causal chain, and you need an aggregation policy that gates the join node on its full dependency set, recorded durably so the completion decision survives a restart. A flat counter could reach its target while the wrong tasks finished or a fan-in input was still missing, and it gives no way to locate a bottleneck at the reducer rather than at a worker.
